summary: This informational document defines a mechanism for reoptimizing loosely routed MPLS and GMPLS traffic engineered LSPs signaled with RSVP-TE. A head-end can trigger path re-evaluation, and a mid-point can tell it a better path exists or that reoptimization is needed, for example for maintenance. It covers intra- and inter-domain cases.

eli5.summary: Your planned trip passed only through a few named towns, with gaps to fill in. This lets the starting point recheck for a better route, or lets a middle stop say please reroute.

questions: how to find better mpls paths
subtitle: Finding better paths in networks split across areas and domains

tldr.problem: Loosely routed MPLS traffic engineering paths specify only some hops explicitly, leaving others to be computed by intermediate routers. When a better path appears in a downstream area or domain, the head-end router cannot see it and continues using a suboptimal path.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines two mechanisms: a head-end LSR can request path re-evaluation at intermediate routers, and mid-point routers can proactively notify the head-end when a better path exists or maintenance is needed, allowing graceful rerouting using the make-before-break procedure.
tldr.outcome: Networks can now detect and use better paths across domain boundaries without disrupting traffic, and routers can signal needed maintenance reroutes to the source.

today: RFC 4736 is an Informational RFC published in November 2006. It remains the primary specification for reoptimization of loosely routed MPLS TE LSPs. Modern MPLS networks, particularly those spanning multiple areas or autonomous systems, implement these mechanisms to detect and use better paths as network topology evolves.

sections.title: Loosely Routed MPLS Paths
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) Traffic Engineering allows network operators to explicitly specify forwarding paths. A path can be strictly routed (every hop specified) or loosely routed (some hops are loose hops, computed by intermediate routers).

A loosely routed path is signaled by RSVP-TE with an Explicit Route Object (ERO) containing one or more loose hops. When a router along the path receives the signal and its next hop is marked loose, it computes a path to that loose hop and forwards the signal downstream. This allows paths to span multiple routing domains or areas where the head-end (starting router) does not have visibility.

However, this flexibility creates a problem: if a better path appears in a downstream domain after the path is established, the head-end router cannot see it because it is in a different routing area or autonomous system. The path continues using a potentially suboptimal route.
sections.eli5: You tell your GPS "go to exit 42, then downtown, then the airport" without specifying every turn. Each interchange fills in the details for its section. But if a better road opens after you start, you don't know about it.

sections.title: Setting Up Loosely Routed Paths
sections.content:
When a head-end router signals a loosely routed LSP, it specifies some hops as strict (directly connected) and others as loose (to be computed by intermediate routers). For example, a path might be specified as: R1 → R3 (loose) → R8 (loose) → R11 (loose).

At each loose hop, the router receiving the signal performs ERO expansion: it computes a path to the next loose hop and fills in the strict hops between them. The R3 router, upon seeing that the next loose hop is R8, computes a path like R3 → R6 → R7 → R8 and adds those strict hops to the signaling message. This process repeats at each loose hop.

The advantage is that each router computes only the segment it sees, using the best information available in its local routing domain. The disadvantage is that topology changes in downstream domains are invisible to the head-end, preventing it from optimizing the overall path.
sections.eli5: You say "pass through these landmarks" but leave the details to whoever's at each landmark. Each person takes the best route they know to the next landmark. But nobody upstream hears about new shortcuts downstream.

sections.title: Detecting and Signaling Better Paths
sections.content:
RFC 4736 defines two complementary mechanisms for reoptimization:

Head-end request function: The head-end router sends a path with the "Path re-evaluation request" flag set in its SESSION-ATTRIBUTE object. When a mid-point router receives this flag and determines that the next loose hop, it performs path re-evaluation: it recomputes the path to the next loose hop and compares the new path's cost to the existing path's cost. If a better (lower-cost) path exists, the mid-point immediately sends an RSVP PathErr message back to the head-end with error code 25 (Notify) and sub-code 6 (Preferable path exists). The head-end can then decide whether to reoptimize using the make-before-break procedure.

Mid-point explicit notification function: Alternatively, a mid-point router can proactively trigger path re-evaluation using its own timer or when a network event occurs (such as a link coming up). If a better path is found, it sends the same PathErr message without waiting for a request from the head-end. Additionally, if a mid-point router detects that a link or node on the current path will require maintenance, it sends a PathErr with sub-code 7 (local link maintenance required) or 8 (local node maintenance required), signaling that the path must be rerouted.
sections.eli5: The starting point can ask "is there a better way?" and intermediate points answer. Or intermediate points can say unprompted "there's a better way" or "we need repairs, please reroute."

sections.title: Signaling Extensions and Operation
sections.content:
The RFC introduces a new flag in the SESSION-ATTRIBUTE object: the Path re-evaluation request flag (0x20). When set, this flag tells all mid-point routers to check whether a better path exists to their next loose hop.

Three new error sub-codes are defined for the RSVP PathErr Notify message (error code 25):

  • Sub-code 6: Preferable path exists—a better path to the next loose hop was found.
  • Sub-code 7: Local link maintenance required—a link on the path will go down for maintenance.
  • Sub-code 8: Local node maintenance required—a node on the path will go down for maintenance.

When a preferable path is found, the recommended behavior is for the mid-point to not propagate the re-evaluation request flag downstream, since the discovery of a better path downstream eliminates the need for further evaluations. However, nodes MAY cache the newly computed path for a short time (default 5 seconds) to reduce computation overhead if the head-end immediately performs a make-before-break reroute.

Multiple reoptimization triggers are supported: timer-based (periodic checks), event-driven (when link state changes), and operator-driven (manual requests).
sections.eli5: A new flag says "check for better routes." Three new error messages say "found one," "link closing," or "node closing." The path can be cached briefly to speed up the reroute.

sections.title: Implementation and Deployment
sections.content:
The mechanisms defined in this RFC are entirely optional. Routers that do not support the new flag or error codes will simply forward the flag unmodified and ignore unfamiliar error messages, allowing graceful coexistence with older implementations.

Head-end routers that do not support the new error sub-codes will silently ignore PathErr messages containing them, allowing mid-point routers to notify without breaking older systems.

Operators can control reoptimization behavior through configuration, such as setting minimum intervals between re-evaluation requests or policies about which mid-point notifications to accept. Boundary routers spanning multiple administrative domains may choose to strip or modify PathErr messages to preserve confidentiality when notifying the head-end across domain boundaries.

The document notes that routers can achieve reoptimization without this mechanism by periodically attempting make-before-break replacements speculatively, though this is less efficient since it cannot detect whether a better path actually exists.
sections.eli5: Older routers ignore the new flags and messages, so new and old can work together. Operators can throttle the reoptimization to avoid too much churn. Domains can hide details from each other.
